result.question:
Survey the best AI/ML-powered tools (as of mid-2026) across these application- and infrastructure-security scanning categories. For EACH category, name the leading tools that genuinely use AI/ML (not just marketing), state concretely what the AI/ML actually does (e.g. reduces false positives, prioritizes exploitable findings, generates fixes, reachability analysis, autonomous exploitation), whether it is open-source or commercial, and bind every claim to a source URL + a supporting quote.

Categories:
1. Web Application Vulnerability Scanning (AI-driven web app scanners).
2. DAST — Dynamic Application Security Testing (running-app black-box scanners with AI).
3. System / Infrastructure Vulnerability Scanning (host, network, cloud, container/image scanning with AI prioritization).
4. SAST — Static Application Security Testing (source-code analysis with AI/LLM: false-positive reduction, autofix, reachability).
5. SCA — Software Composition Analysis (open-source dependency / SBOM / transitive-CVE analysis with AI, reachability, auto-remediation).

For each category also call out: which tool is the strongest AI-native option, what specifically the AI contributes over traditional rule/signature scanning, and any notable limitations or skepticism about the AI claims. Conclude with a short cross-category view of where AI is actually moving the needle in security scanning vs where it is hype.
result.summary: As of mid-2026, AI/ML is genuinely reshaping security scanning primarily through reachability-and-context reasoning that reduces false positives and prioritizes exploitable findings — this is where the strongest, best-evidenced value lies (Endor Labs AI SAST's multi-agent call-graph/dataflow reachability, Semgrep's dataflow reachability cutting high/critical FPs "up to 98%," and Datadog Bits AI classifying SAST findings as true/false positives by reading code context). A second real frontier is LLM-augmented detection that extends beyond pattern matching to business-logic flaws, IDORs, and broken authorization (Semgrep Multimodal), and autonomous multi-agent pentest frameworks driving standard offensive tools (xOffense on a fine-tuned Qwen3-32B). However, the hardest capability — LLMs reliably detecting vulnerabilities from raw code — is largely hype: independent benchmarks show fine-tuned LLMs at near-random detection (52.1%, ~2pts above chance), "calibration without comprehension," and general-purpose models "akin to random guessing" on leakage-corrected benchmarks; a 2026 vendor survey found 78% of security teams hit critical false negatives from fully automated scanning. The pattern that consistently works is hybrid: a conservative traditional SAST scanner feeding an LLM to triage/extend results (raw-LSAST reached 68.89% TP-rate vs 17.91% for a raw LLM), while added complexity like RAG can hurt. Net: AI moves the needle on prioritization, false-positive filtering, and reachability today; autonomous end-to-end vulnerability discovery remains an open research question, not a settled capability.

findings.claim: SAST with AI reachability/multi-agent reasoning is the strongest, best-evidenced AI-native category — prioritizing exploitable findings over signature matching. Endor Labs AI SAST applies a call-graph/dataflow reachability engine to first-party code via a multi-agent system; Semgrep Multimodal blends static analysis with LLM reasoning to catch IDORs, broken authorization, and business-logic flaws beyond pattern matching.
findings.evidence: Endor: 'applies a reachability engine... to first-party code via a multi-agent system... call-graph and dataflow analysis to trace how data moves... prioritizing vulnerabilities that are actually reachable and exploitable.' Semgrep: 'blends static analysis with AI reasoning to find OWASP risks, business logic flaws, and IDORs.' Both are commercial. Endor's specific '2.6x more vulnerabilities' and '60% fewer FPs' benchmark figures were REFUTED (0-3) as self-benchmark cherry-picking; only the architecture claim survives. Semgrep's self-reported efficacy figures (8x TPs, 61% precision) are unreplicated.

findings.claim: AI-driven false-positive reduction is the clearest place AI moves the needle. Semgrep SCA reachability reduces high/critical FPs by up to 98% by identifying exploitable dependencies; Datadog Bits AI (LLM) classifies SAST findings as likely true/false positive by evaluating code context rule-based analysis cannot; LLM-agent FP filtering (Aider/OpenHands/SWE-agent) cut FP rate from 92%+ to as low as 6.3%.
findings.evidence: Semgrep SCA: reachability 'reducing false positives in high and critical severity findings by up to 98%' (vendor 'up to' best-case). Datadog: LLM evaluates 'how data moves through functions, how input is validated, and whether conditions for exploitation are actually met.' 'Sifting the Noise' (arXiv 2601.22952, Jan 2026) compares LLM agents on OWASP Benchmark + Java, reducing FP rate to as low as 6.3% — but warns low FP may mask high false-negatives. All commercial except the study.

findings.claim: DAST/autonomous offensive testing: xOffense is an AI-driven autonomous multi-agent penetration-testing framework on a fine-tuned open-source LLM (Qwen3-32B), with specialized recon/vuln-scan/exploitation agents under an orchestration layer. The AI's concrete contribution is Chain-of-Thought-fine-tuned reasoning that generates precise tool commands and drives standard offensive tooling autonomously.
findings.evidence: Open-source model (Qwen3-32B) fine-tuned on CoT pentest data; 'assigns specialized agents to reconnaissance, vulnerability scanning, and exploitation, with an orchestration layer.' Skepticism: non-peer-reviewed preprint; 79.17% benchmark self-reported; the specific tool list (Nmap/Nikto/Metasploit/SQLMap) is an unsourced elaboration not in the abstract. Illustrates the research direction for AI DAST rather than a proven commercial product.

findings.claim: The hybrid pattern — traditional scanner feeding an LLM — is what actually works; added complexity like RAG can hurt. Passing conservative SAST (open-source Bearer) output into an LLM and instructing it to find only NEW vulnerabilities raised TP-rate from 17.91% (raw LLM) to 68.89% with 86.11% precision (raw-LSAST). Adding a RAG knowledge-retrieval layer (HackerOne reports) was counterproductive, underperforming the SAST-only approach.
findings.evidence: 'passing the Bearer findings to the LLM significantly increases the capabilities of LLMs in finding vulnerabilities.' 'using a RAG infrastructure for knowledge retrieval can be counterproductive.' raw-LSAST F1 76.54% vs Combined-LSAST (with RAG) 49.18%. This is the strongest evidence for AI-augmented rather than AI-autonomous scanning.

findings.claim: HYPE CHECK: standalone LLM vulnerability DETECTION is largely unreliable — near-random on hard benchmarks, non-robust, and prone to false positives on patched code. Fine-tuned LLMs best detection 52.1% (~2pts above chance), exact CWE Top-1 <1.3%; fine-tuning is 'calibration without comprehension' (shifts thresholds without building security reasoning). Earlier work: 8 LLMs incl. GPT-4/PaLM2 flagged patched code as still vulnerable; renaming vars flipped answers 26%/17% of the time.
findings.evidence: 'best detection score reached only 52.1%, roughly 2 points above chance... current LLMs lack reliable security reasoning for systems software, regardless of fine-tuning strategy.' 'Fine-tuning shifts the output threshold without changing the decision policy... the underlying security reasoning remains absent.' SecLLMHolmes (IEEE S&P 2024): 'all models... have a high false positive rate, and flag code where vulnerabilities have been patched as still vulnerable.' Scoped mainly to systems/kernel C and 2023-era-to-2026 models.

findings.claim: HYPE CHECK: LLM-scanner 'deeper reasoning' claims lack independent validation, and rankings are metric- and author-dependent. On RealVuln (26 real Python repos), under recall-weighted F3, security-specialized Kolega.Dev (73.0) and best general LLM Claude Sonnet 4.6 (51.7) beat best rule-based Semgrep (17.7) ~3x — but the benchmark is authored by Kolega, and under F1 Sonnet (60.9) beats Kolega (52.4), so '3x dominance' is metric-dependent. The paper itself frames the skepticism: no open benchmark existed to confirm LLM scanners deliver rather than trade one failure mode for another.
findings.evidence: 'Under F3, the Security-Specialized scanner Kolega.Dev (73.0) leads, followed by the best General-Purpose LLM, Claude Sonnet 4.6 (51.7)... nearly 3x higher than the best Rule-Based tool, Semgrep (17.7).' 'no open benchmark exists to test whether LLM-based scanners actually deliver on these promises, or just trade one set of failure modes for another.' Conflict of interest: winning tool = benchmark author.

findings.claim: Traditional AND fully-automated scanning both have severe real-world false-positive/false-negative problems that AI is being sold to fix. Ghost Security: 99.5% FP rate for command-injection in Python/Flask (91% FP overall across ~2,166 findings). Fluid Attacks: best fully automated tool detected only 22.7% of known vulns (avg F2 1.9% across 36 scanners). Cobalt 2026 survey (455 pros): 78% of teams reported automated tools missing critical vulns / returning false negatives.
findings.evidence: 'Ghost Security CAST report found a 99.5% false positive rate for command-injection findings in Python/Flask... Fluid Attacks benchmark showed the best fully automated tool found only 22.7%... F2 score of just 1.9% across 36 scanners.' Cobalt: '78% of organizations... fully automated scanning tools missing critical vulnerabilities and returning false negatives.' Caveat: Ghost/Fluid/Cobalt are all vendors with commercial incentive; cite as vendor benchmarks. A related Cobalt claim (trust in full automation collapsed 29%->9%) was REFUTED 0-3.

findings.claim: AI code-generation agents (adjacent risk surface) mostly fail to produce correct-and-secure code, expanding the attack surface scanners must cover. Best agent (SWE-agent + DeepSeek-V3.1) produced correct-and-secure solutions on only 15.2% of tasks (9.2% average); among functionally correct outputs ~70% still had security issues, and agents introduced 14 CWE types including some never previously recorded.
findings.evidence: 'Best combination (SWE-agent + DeepSeek-V3.1) achieved only 15.2% correct-and-secure solutions; average was just 9.2%.' 'Among functionally correct... roughly 70% still had security issues... Agents introduced 14 CWE types... some never previously seen.' Measures code generation, not scanning, but underscores why AI-written code needs AI-aware scanning.

findings.claim: Cross-category consensus: whether LLMs can reliably detect vulnerabilities remains an OPEN research question, not a settled capability — reinforcing that AI's proven value today is in triage/prioritization/reachability, not autonomous discovery.
findings.evidence: ICSE 2025 'Vulnerability Detection with Code Language Models: How Far Are We?' (arXiv 2403.18624) — on leakage-corrected PrimeVul a SOTA 7B model dropped from 68.26% F1 (BigVul) to 3.09% F1; GPT-3.5/GPT-4 'akin to random guessing' (FNR ~90%). Multiple corroborating surveys (2502.07049, 2507.22659) echo the unresolved status.

result.caveats: Coverage is uneven by category: SAST and SCA have the deepest, most independently-benchmarked evidence; DAST/autonomous pentest rests largely on a single non-peer-reviewed preprint (xOffense); and dedicated System/Infrastructure/cloud/container-image AI scanning (e.g., Wiz, Snyk container, Aqua/Trivy AI prioritization) was NOT independently corroborated in the surviving claims — treat that category as under-covered here. Many efficacy figures are vendor self-reported 'up to' marketing numbers (Semgrep 98%, Endor's refuted 2.6x, Cobalt/Ghost/Fluid vendor surveys) rather than independent replication; the RealVuln benchmark that most favors LLM/specialized scanners is authored by the winning tool's own vendor (Kolega) and is metric-dependent (F3 vs F1 flip the ranking). Time-sensitivity is high: negative LLM-detection findings (52.1% near-random, 'calibration without comprehension') are scoped to specific models/domains (notably Linux-kernel systems C) and 2023-2026 model generations, so frontier-model capability may shift quickly. Five claims were adversarially REFUTED (Endor 2.6x and 60%-fewer-FP benchmark figures, Semgrep 80%-fewer-FP triage, a blanket 'LLMs not ready' generalization, and Cobalt's 29%->9% trust-collapse stat) — excluded from findings.
openQuestions: Which tools lead AI-driven System/Infrastructure, cloud, network, and container/image scanning (Wiz, Snyk, Aqua/Trivy, Prisma) and what does their AI concretely contribute? This category was not independently corroborated in the verified claims.

Do frontier-model generations (2026+) close the near-random vulnerability-DETECTION gap, or does 'calibration without comprehension' persist beyond systems/kernel C into web-app and multi-language code?

Is there any vendor-independent, leakage-controlled benchmark comparing commercial AI SAST/SCA tools (Endor, Semgrep, Snyk, Datadog) head-to-head, given that current wins come from self-authored benchmarks?

For SCA specifically, how do AI/reachability-based auto-remediation and transitive-CVE fix generation perform in practice (real merge/fix acceptance rates) versus the reachability-prioritization claims that are well-evidenced?

refuted.claim: In an 8-project benchmark, Endor Labs AI SAST found 192 real vulnerabilities — 2.6x what Claude Opus 4.7 caught, 3.5x what Codex GPT-5.5 caught, and 2.4x what Semgrep OSS found.
Endor Labs AI SAST produced about 60% fewer false positives than Semgrep OSS and OpenGrep, which each flagged over 460; industry benchmarks estimate 68-78% of SAST findings are false positives.
Semgrep's AI-assisted triage lets AppSec teams triage 80% fewer false positives across SAST and SCA.
LLMs fail at detecting vulnerabilities in real-world projects, indicating they are not yet ready for automated vulnerability detection.
Trust in relying entirely on AI automation for security testing collapsed from 29% to 9% year-over-year, with 47% now preferring a hybrid human+AI model.
